video_title: Why I Just Bought A House (For The 1st Time In My Life At Age 55) | Adam Taggart & Melody Wright
gist: Thoughtful Money host Adam Taggart, a lifelong renter who called the 2000s housing bubble and then sat out the market for two decades, is interviewed by housing analyst Melody Wright about buying his first home at 55 — a Toll Brothers new build on a ridge in South Reno, Nevada. The conversation is less a market call than a granular teardown of new-build developer economics (design-center markups, made-up lot premiums, commission and property-tax basis games), mortgage structure (a 6.7% quote, sub-25% LTV, a possible ARM he intends to prepay), and the local-versus-national divergence that let him buy into a submarket he expects to fall ~5% while Wright and Nick Gerli still forecast a multi-year national downtrend.

themes.theme: A Two-Decade Housing Sit-Out And Why It Ended

insights.claim: Adam Taggart, host of the Thoughtful Money channel, bought his first home ever at age 55 in South Reno, Nevada, after renting his entire life and deliberately sitting out the US housing market since roughly 2004.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A prominent housing bear capitulating on his own residence is a sentiment datapoint worth logging — and he explicitly frames it as a personal, not a market, decision.

insights.claim: Taggart's original 2004-05 housing bubble call was triggered by bottom-up transaction absurdity: teardown-grade starter homes in Palo Alto / Menlo Park were roughly $800,000 twenty-three years ago and his realtor told him he had to overbid asking by at least $100,000, after which sellers repeatedly took other offers without even inviting a counter.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Bidding behavior at the entry rung of a market — mandatory overbids with no counteroffer invitation — is the same late-cycle tell to watch in today's tight submarkets.
insights.quote: Just so you know, if you want the home, you're going to have to over bid for it. Um, probably by at least $100,000.

insights.claim: Taggart says the conviction to sit out came from failing to find the bull case: he went looking online for the reason he *should* buy and instead found the housing-bubble warnings, which converted a gut discomfort into a multi-year positioning decision.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Actively hunting for the argument against your own instinct — and failing to find it — is a usable conviction test before a large illiquid commitment.
insights.quote: I think my gut feeling was right, that um it's not worth buying homes. Uh that the price is high, the value was low.

insights.claim: The expensive half of Taggart's correct bubble call was the re-entry, not the exit: he moved to Sonoma County in July 2012 almost exactly as housing bottomed, chose to rent to test the location, and by 2014 Northern California prices were back at 2007 levels — after which he waited another decade for a correction that never arrived.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: The canonical failure mode of a correct bearish macro call is the missing re-entry rule; a right-for-years thesis still lost him a full cycle of housing appreciation.
insights.quote: we moved in 2012 in this in July of 2012, so right mid year, which was pretty much right as the housing market was just starting to rebound. And that's when I should have bought, but we didn't

insights.claim: Taggart admits his housing bearishness became personal rather than analytical — he framed it as outlasting the market itself — which is how a valuation view calcifies into an identity that blocks re-entry.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A self-aware confession of thesis-as-identity from a professional commentator; the tell is when the position is described in adversarial terms rather than price terms.
insights.quote: I'm going to have greater lasting power than you, the market.

insights.claim: What finally forced Taggart's decision was exogenous, not analytical: his landlord accepted an unsolicited offer on the Reno house he was renting, ending the lease and converting an open-ended wait into a hard deadline.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Renters holding out for a correction have no natural forcing function; the decision typically gets made for them by a landlord's exit, on the landlord's timing rather than the market's.
insights.quote: we got an unsolicited offer for the house that we're taking. So, I'm really sorry, but you guys are going to have to move out at the end of the month.

insights.claim: Taggart's mechanism for making a multi-decade wait survivable was a dedicated 'home fund' he kept funding every year he did not buy, so the percentage of a house he could purchase outright kept rising even as prices rose past him.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: For anyone priced out, compounding a segregated down-payment pool is the only lever that improves affordability independent of whether the market cooperates.
insights.quote: every year I when I didn't buy, I made sure that I was shoveling as much as I could into a home fund.

insights.claim: Taggart's bull case for South Reno is tax-arbitrage in-migration: Nevada's zero state income tax and lower cost of living are pulling wealthy Californians, and he cites California's newly proposed wealth tax as an accelerant to that flow.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: State tax policy is the demand driver for zero-income-tax border markets; a California wealth tax would be a direct catalyst for Reno, Las Vegas and similar destination housing.
insights.quote: California keeps making more and more reasons for the productive its productive residents to leave um especially now with the the wealth tax that's been um proposed.

insights.claim: Taggart measured the in-migration through absorption rather than price: inventory in his South Reno target zips was low and he estimated two or three newly arrived Californians were hunting for every house that came to market in a given month.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Buyer-per-listing absorption is the leading indicator in migration-driven submarkets; price prints lag it and national inventory data will not show it.
insights.quote: for every house that came on, there were probably two or three new Californians that had just moved in that month looking for a place to live.

insights.claim: Reno's economic base has broadened from casinos into a tech and industrial cluster — Taggart names a Tesla gigafactory, an Nvidia data-center presence, and healthcare — driving 10 to 15 years of population growth that Californians still discount via what he calls 'the Reno sneer'.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Persistent reputational lag between an employment base and public perception is exactly where housing mispricing lives; watch other secondary metros with new hyperscaler and gigafactory anchors.
insights.quote: the town has exploded in size over the past 10 to 15 years as a bunch of really big tech companies and other industries have come into the state.

insights.claim: Taggart treats water security as a formal screen for a forever home and argues Reno is structurally advantaged because it sits directly against the Sierra and is the first place snowmelt runoff hits, giving predictable groundwater as long as the snowpack persists.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Water rights and hydrology are becoming a first-order housing variable in the Southwest; proximity to the runoff source, not state-level supply, is what actually differentiates.
insights.quote: it's always going to have groundwater for as long as it snows in the Sierra, right? As long as there's snow pack to melt during the year, Nevada is actually going to be very rich in water.

insights.claim: Melody Wright flags data-center buildout as the emerging threat to water supply and quality of life in exactly these resource-advantaged destination markets, and tells new residents to get involved in local politics early enough to influence permitting outcomes.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Data-center siting is becoming a local housing risk factor — competing for water and power in the same secondary metros retail buyers are migrating into.
insights.quote: they don't start building a data center, you know, two miles down the road or whatever.

insights.claim: Wright uses Asheville as the cautionary case against 'climate haven' migration narratives: it drew inflows on abundant water and climate-refuge branding and then took a flood unlike anything in a hundred years.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Climate-haven branding is now itself a demand driver — and a crowding risk — in secondary housing markets; the tail risk that the branding denies is the one that repriced Asheville.
insights.quote: a lot of people move into Asheville because it was actually people talked about it as a climate haven

themes.theme: Zip-Code Divergence Against A National Downtrend

insights.claim: Taggart states that his own regularly featured housing analysts still expect the national housing market to keep trending down for a couple more years and to be relatively substantial by the time the correction finishes — a bearish national view he is not retracting despite buying.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: The national bear case on the channel is unchanged; treat this purchase as a submarket call, not a signal that the national forecast has flipped.
insights.quote: you still believe it's probably likely going to keep continuing trending down for a couple years from now. Um and be relatively substantial by the time the dust settles.

insights.claim: Nick Gerli's Reventure app forecasts Taggart's specific South Reno zip code to *increase* in price next year, showing zip-level models can invert the sign of a bearish national housing call.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Zip-level forecasting tools are the operative resolution for housing decisions; a national or even metro-level bearish print is not actionable for a specific purchase.
insights.quote: Nick's reventure app, you know, predicts that the zip code that I'm in is actually likely to increase next year.

insights.claim: Taggart's own downside scenario for his South Reno submarket is roughly a 5% decline, versus the 20-30% drawdowns he considers plausible elsewhere — an explicit statement of how wide he thinks intra-national housing dispersion has become.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A 5% versus 20-30% spread between submarkets in the same correction means national housing indices will badly misprice any individual decision.
insights.quote: Prices sure could come down. I don't see them coming down 20 30%. you know, maybe they come down 5%.

insights.claim: Melody Wright's pushback is that local price resilience is a function of embedded leverage rather than desirability, and she says she has examined the leverage in that Reno development and believes some of those owners will be forced to sell.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Screen destination submarkets by owner leverage and financing mix, not by amenity or migration narrative — forced supply is what actually breaks a resilient-looking zip.
insights.quote: Depends on how much leverage is out there, Adam.

insights.claim: Taggart counters that the marginal buyer in his ridge development is unusually low-leverage — older, wealthier, sometimes buying it as a second or ski home rather than a primary residence — which changes the forced-selling math relative to a typical 20%-down tract.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Cash-heavy second-home buyers make a submarket price-insensitive on the way down but also thin on the way up; the correct screen is buyer financing mix, which is observable in deed records.
insights.quote: They're not putting 20% down is is my assumption.

insights.claim: Supply scarcity, not price, drove Taggart's timing: only about two dozen homes are being built on his ridge with the surrounding land staying open space permanently, so waiting for a correction risked a five- to ten-year wait for the next comparable unit.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: When a target asset has a fixed, tiny float, timing the price cycle is dominated by inventory-availability risk — the option to buy later may simply not exist.
insights.quote: there's only like I think maybe like two dozen homes that are being built up in the area uh where I am, and the rest is going to be open space forever.

insights.claim: Taggart's scarcity framework is that migration manufactures buyers but not the scarce input those buyers want — more wealthy Californians will arrive in Reno, but the supply of premium views is permanently fixed.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: In migration markets, underwrite the non-replicable attribute (view, waterfront, ski access) rather than the structure — that is the component that captures the demand shock.
insights.quote: they're going to make a lot more rich Californians fleeing California. What they're not going to make more of is fantastic views.

insights.claim: Taggart reports that Toll Brothers makes the majority of its money on a home not from the base price but from the design-center selections the buyer picks, sold from a restricted in-house menu at hefty markups.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Homebuilder gross margin sits in the options attach rate, not the sticker — a lever that can hold reported margins up even as base prices are discounted into a weak market.
insights.quote: Toll Brothers makes the majority of their money on the house from the design elements that you pick.

insights.claim: The developer's price stack has three separate layers — the quoted house price, a discretionary 'lot premium' Taggart says is essentially a made-up number (a couple hundred thousand dollars in his case), and then the design-center upgrades on top.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Advertised new-build base prices are not comparable to resale comps; the lot premium is pure discretionary pricing power that flexes with demand and disappears first when it fades.
insights.quote: there's kind of three different values. Um there's what they price the house at. Um, then there's what they call the lot premium on top of it, which is essentially a number they just make up

insights.claim: The developer's advertised payment of the buyer's agent commission is calculated only off the base house price, excluding both the lot premium and all upgrades — so in Taggart's case the builder covers roughly half of what the agent is actually owed.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: 'We pay your realtor' is a partial subsidy at new-build developments; buyers should compute the commission base before assuming the cost is covered.
insights.quote: they're probably paying like half of it, right? Um, but I'm still thrilled that I only have to pay 50%

insights.claim: Shifting line items from the developer's design center to outside contractors permanently lowers the delivered price of the home, which lowers both the realtor commission base and the property-tax basis for the life of ownership — a benefit that exists even when the outside price is identical.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: The tax-basis effect makes contractor substitution positive-NPV even at price parity; this is a concrete, repeatable saving for anyone buying a production new build.
insights.quote: there are benefits, long-term benefits you get from reducing the price of the home at handoff to you. Um because that reduces your property taxes forever

insights.claim: Production builders bar buyer-hired contractors from the site until the keys are handed over and are obligated to deliver a live-in-ready house, so base-grade flooring and cabinetry get installed and then immediately ripped out and discarded by buyers substituting their own finishes.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A structural source of embedded material waste and duplicated cost in production homebuilding — and a real friction cost (months of non-occupancy) buyers should price into a new-build timeline.
insights.quote: So, it's just it's bananas the waste that's involved here.

insights.claim: Taggart got into a development that had priced him out by taking over a lot abandoned by an earlier buyer: because the layout was already locked and permitted, the developer priced that unit materially below the other lots in exchange for zero structural flexibility.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Abandoned or re-traded lots are a recurring discount channel at sold-out developments — a reason to keep calling a builder's sales office rather than watching listings.
insights.quote: because this one is is already kind of set in stone, at least in terms of its structural layout

insights.claim: Taggart still paid roughly 10-15% above the maximum budget he had set for himself, having concluded from two months of comparison shopping that nothing else available matched the property.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Even a disciplined, cash-heavy, decades-patient buyer broke his own budget ceiling once he had a comparison set — a candid illustration of how weak price anchors are against scarcity.
insights.quote: it was still outside my budget, but it was like, you know, probably 10 15% out of what I thought my max was.

insights.claim: Taking over a mid-stream lot compressed the decision window from months to about two and a half weeks for hundreds of design-center choices, because the build schedule was already moving on a preset production line.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: The discount on a re-traded lot is partly paid in decision-quality risk; buyers should budget advisory help specifically for that compressed window.
insights.quote: Now you've got like two and a half weeks

insights.claim: Model and demonstration homes are deliberately loaded with hundreds of thousands of dollars of upgrades and, per Taggart's experience, sometimes with finishes the builder does not even sell — making them a pure price-anchoring device rather than a baseline.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Treat the model home as a marketing anchor, not a spec; the delta between it and base finish is the builder's upgrade revenue opportunity.
insights.quote: It's just got hundreds and hundreds of thousands of upgrades here.

insights.claim: Taggart's countermeasure to design-center markups was to hire an independent design firm to attend the selection meetings and then run every Toll Brothers line-item estimate past a builder with 20-plus years in Reno to identify which items outside contractors could beat on price or quality.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A repeatable playbook: get the builder's itemized estimate, price-check it against local trades, and substitute selectively — the advisory fee is small against the markup recovered.

insights.claim: Melody Wright's new-build oversight advice is to document the build photographically from foundation onward and to commission an independent inspection at each completed milestone rather than relying on the builder's own quality sign-off.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Milestone inspections are the only leverage a buyer has on quality before handover, when defects become the owner's problem.

insights.claim: Taggart was quoted around 6.7% on a 30-year mortgage and expects rates to trend down shortly after he locks — his mortgage does not start until roughly next July — and then to trend higher over the longer term.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A near-7% 30-year quote is the current cost of carry for a well-qualified borrower; his down-then-up rate path implies a refinance window before a secular rise.
insights.quote: we got a quote for the 30, right? And and that was coming in, I think at the time, like around 6.7, so close to 7%.

insights.claim: Taggart underwrote to a standard 20%-down approval but expects to actually borrow 25% or less of the home's value and to be mortgage-free within a couple of years of taking the loan.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: The purchase is effectively an all-cash transaction with a bridge loan — which is why he can hold a bearish national housing view and still buy without drawdown risk.
insights.quote: I'm pretty confident that when I when I take out the mortgage, it's going to be for 25% or less of the value of the house.

insights.claim: Taggart rejects the popular 'inflate away the mortgage' argument he debated with Lance Roberts, holding that a mortgage simply makes the house more expensive unless the borrower has a rock-solid way to earn above the mortgage cost for the entire life of the loan.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the widely repeated 'debt is short the dollar' housing thesis: the carry trade only works with a reliable spread over the mortgage rate, which most households do not have.
insights.quote: unless you have a pretty rockolid way to generate a return above your mortgage cost for, you know, as long as you have a mortgage. If you can do that, that makes sense.

insights.claim: Because he intends to prepay quickly, Taggart says he may take an adjustable-rate mortgage despite generally advising against them — reset risk is irrelevant if the loan is retired before the first adjustment.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: For borrowers with a credible short payoff horizon, the ARM's lower initial coupon is nearly free optionality — a structure most US buyers reflexively rule out.
insights.quote: I actually might take on an ARM uh an adjustable rate mortgage because I'm confident I'm going to pay the mortgage off before the ARM would reate.

insights.claim: Melody Wright argues US borrowers wrongly stigmatize ARMs because of GFC memory, noting most other countries run five- to seven-year adjustable products, and that the American 30-year fixed only functions because of a securitization machine she considers unhealthy for the economy.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: A structural critique of the US housing finance system from a 20-year mortgage practitioner: the fixed-rate norm is a policy artifact whose cost is a giant securitization apparatus.
insights.quote: We are the geniuses, and I say that very sarcastically, of the 30-year mortgage. and that we've made that work by uh creating this very large securization machine behind it which has been in my opinion very unhealthy for the economy.

insights.claim: Wright's underwriting framework is that the loan product type is secondary — what actually determines risk is the amount of leverage, whether the borrower understands the product, and whether it fits their situation, rather than the interest-only or adjustable label.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Reframes mortgage credit risk analysis away from product labels toward LTV and borrower fit — the same lens that separates 2005 originations from safe adjustable lending.
insights.quote: It's like what really matters is how much leverage. Do you understand this product? Does this product make sense for you?

insights.claim: Wright argues US lending has degraded into what she calls 'Henry Ford credit' — forcing borrowers into standardized product boxes instead of sitting down to match a structure to their savings, job, leverage and life goals — and that the damage compounds when those loans are rehypothecated into thousands of derivatives.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: The mass-production of standardized mortgage product is what makes securitization possible and underwriting quality unobservable — the same mechanism that turned a housing downturn systemic in 2008.
insights.quote: we continue to try to Henry Ford credit um not know our customers

insights.claim: Mortgage approval was a non-event for a high-income, high-savings buyer — a broker quote inside 48 hours — but Toll Brothers still required Taggart to apply to its own lending arm, ostensibly as a creditworthiness screen and in practice as a sales channel for the loan.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Builder financial-services arms capture mortgage revenue through a mandatory application step; buyers are not obligated to take the loan and should shop it independently.
insights.quote: obtaining the mortgage was almost a nothing burger

insights.claim: Taggart notes every counterparty in a home purchase is incentive-conflicted — the realtor is paid on closing and the mortgage broker is paid on the longest revenue stream — so hiring an advisor with no stake in the transaction is the structural fix.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Applies the fee-only fiduciary logic from wealth management to the largest single transaction most households make, where no such advisory category currently exists.
insights.quote: your realtor just wants the damn deal to close so he gets his commission.

insights.claim: A viewer alerted Taggart that lender-required title insurance protects only the lender and lapses when the mortgage is paid off or refinanced, so buyers should ask for an owner's endorsement raising the policy amount to the purchase price to keep their equity covered afterward.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A cheap, widely unknown protection gap: the borrower who pays for title insurance is not the party it insures, and the coverage disappears exactly when their equity is largest.
insights.quote: The title insurance only protects the lender.

insights.claim: An ALTA enhanced or expanded homeowner's title policy adds roughly 23 additional covered risks beyond a standard owner's policy, including protections extending past the closing date — and Taggart found it was already bundled into his Toll Brothers closing costs without anyone flagging it.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Standard owner's policies cover only defects predating closing; the enhanced version is inexpensive and its presence or absence is buried in closing paperwork nobody reads.
insights.quote: the homeowner's policy adds roughly 23 extra covered risks, including unique protections that extend after you buy the home.

insights.claim: A buyer using an agent must bring that agent to the very first meeting with a new-build developer, because developers refuse to register — and therefore refuse to pay — an agent introduced after the buyer discovered the property alone.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A single procedural misstep on a first sales-office visit permanently forfeits the developer-paid share of the buyer-agent commission — a five-figure error.
insights.quote: you have to have your realtor come with you at your first meeting with with that developer

insights.claim: The attribute Taggart bought the house for — an unobstructed Sierra view — is protected only by an HOA rule barring second stories on the homes below, a rule the developer conceded a future homeowner-controlled board could amend.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: View premiums in new developments are secured by amendable private covenants, not zoning — meaning the scarcity being paid for is only as durable as a future HOA vote.
insights.quote: the HOA prevents that right now, but in the future, somebody might change the HOA rules

insights.claim: Wright's remedy for HOA amendment risk is for buyers in aggressive-HOA communities to join the board themselves rather than rely on covenants staying put, and both speakers say HOA documents are the paperwork most worth reading line by line with an experienced agent.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Governance participation is the only actual control a buyer has over the private rules that determine their property's value; it is free and almost nobody does it.
insights.quote: go ahead and get on the board. Um, you know, get involved

insights.claim: Taggart's decision filter for hundreds of minor new-build choices is whether the item can be easily changed after handover — pre-wiring, outlet placement, HVAC and plumbing cost hundreds to low thousands during framing but require demolition to retrofit and also raise resale value.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A clean rule for prioritizing spend under time pressure: buy the irreversible items, defer the reversible ones — the same optionality logic as any sunk-cost decision.
insights.quote: is this something that I can easily address after we get the house

insights.claim: Melody Wright's single gating question for any prospective buyer is whether they are willing to take a loss on the property, and over what holding period — and she says a 'no' answer is the signal not to buy.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: A one-question stress test that separates buyers with genuine holding capacity from those relying on price appreciation to bail out the decision.
insights.quote: are you willing to take a loss at this point, you know, and that's where a lot of people will say no?

insights.claim: Both speakers argue the worst possible housing decision is buying something that requires everything to go right, and that anyone stretching should keep renting and keep funding a house fund, since affordability improves over time even if the market never corrects.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Reframes the rent-versus-buy decision around fragility rather than price forecasting — the correct trigger to buy is a mortgage that is trivially serviceable, not a market bottom.
insights.quote: the worst decision you can make is to buy something that you cannot afford. Um or that everything has to go right for you to be able to continue in.

insights.claim: Wright's sequencing rule is location-first: pick the neighborhood you actually want before looking at what is available, because the dominant failure mode she sees is buyers falling for a house within two hours of seeing it without knowing the commute or the area.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Inverts the standard search process — inventory-first searching is what manufactures the FOMO that produces overpayment.
insights.quote: Where do you want to be? Go pick it.

insights.claim: Wright says new-build sales operations are engineered specifically to break buyer discipline — every aspect designed to get the buyer to pay a little more and to feel they must have it — and buyers should walk in expecting that.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: The sales process, not the market, is the primary source of overpayment at production developments; pre-committing to a spec list is the only defense.
insights.quote: You're basically like walking into a lion's den when you go into these places and you have to keep your head cool about it.

insights.claim: Taggart explicitly refuses to generalize his purchase into a market call, saying it was the right time for him and his wife specifically and that an uncomfortable number of US locations are still trending down and likely to keep doing so for a while.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Guards against reading a well-known bear's home purchase as a bottom signal — his national view is unchanged and his purchase is an idiosyncratic submarket exception.
insights.quote: there are an uncomfortable number of uh locations across the US right now where the trends are downward and likely to continue being downward for a while.

insights.claim: Taggart identifies an unserved market: 'location realtors' rather than house realtors — advisors who help mobile buyers select a metro or neighborhood on tax, water, appreciation and lifestyle criteria before any property search begins.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A structural gap in residential real-estate services: agents are compensated on transactions in a market they already serve, so nobody is paid to help a buyer choose the market itself.
insights.quote: there should be realtors out there that are location realtors, not house realtors.

insights.claim: Wright's closing caution is that buyers cannot mitigate every risk and should not expect to — the Asheville flood being her example — so the right standard is best-available due diligence at the time, not perfect foresight.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: An antidote to analysis paralysis in illiquid personal-asset decisions: the goal is a defensible process, not an unfalsifiable forecast.
insights.quote: we're never going to be able to mitigate every single risk
